name: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
school: Early scholasticism (nominalism vs. realism on universals)
biography: Leader of the twelfth-century mystical movement, Cistercian abbot of Clairvaux from 1115; brought unjust accusations of heresy against Abelard, secured his condemnation at Sens in 1141; hugely influential in ecclesiastical politics (combating antipopes and heresy, preaching the Second Crusade); sought religious truth in subjective contemplation rather than reasoning, and wrote Latin hymns of real beauty despite Russell's judgment that his saintliness 'did not suffice to make him intelligent.'
russell_view: Russell presents the twelfth century as a genuinely creative period that did not recognize its own originality, since every party (Emperor, papacy, Lombard cities, scholastics, Crusaders) legitimized itself by appeal to supposed ancient precedent even while doing something new. He is admiring of the intellectual daring of early scholastics like Abelard, praising his treatment of universals as still philosophically respectable by modern standards, while criticizing the scholastic method's characteristic defects (excessive trust in dialectic over observation, verbal hairsplitting) as more extreme than in Plato. Russell is notably unsympathetic to Saint Bernard, whom he credits with genuine religious feeling and fine Latin hymns but faults for intelligence, unfairness to Abelard, and a naive view of Crusading war as sustainable by religious enthusiasm alone -- captured in Russell's pointed remark, quoting the Encyclopaedia Britannica, that Bernard's greatness 'lay not in the qualities of his intellect, but of his character.'
why_this_matters: Four bound-together twelfth-century developments -- imperial-papal conflict, the rise of the Lombard cities, the Crusades, and scholasticism -- all culminate in the thirteenth century. Roscelin, the first strict scholastic, held a nominalist view of universals that got him into trouble over the Trinity; he recanted at Rheims in 1092.
